consensus_summary: Door/gate primarily signifies access to God and salvation through Jesus Christ, with contextual extensions involving admission, exclusion, heavenly access, ministry opportunity, and authority.
book_summary: Jesus is the threshold into the covenant house and the destination of the Way; the entry also connects doorway posts with blood and God's word and interprets heavenly gates as constellation points through which the New Moon appears.
consensus_core_identification: Jesus Christ is the door or gate through whom one enters salvation and fellowship with God.
book_core_identification: Jesus is the threshold through which one enters the covenant house.
boundary_disagreement: The shared Christological identification is preserved, but the book extends the image into a covenant-house system involving blood- and word-marked posts and, most distinctively, astronomical gates associated with constellations and the New Moon. The astronomical application is not represented in the consensus responses.
material_contradiction: None. The book does not deny that Christ is the saving door; it restates that identification in covenant-house language and adds further applications.
rationale: At minimum core, 'Christ as access to salvation' and 'Jesus as threshold into the covenant house' identify the same central referent and function. The result is REFINED rather than DIVERGENT because no referent is replaced. It is not a pure MATCH because the book makes a substantive additional claim that heavenly gates correspond to constellation-based New Moon passage points, materially broadening the symbol's extension beyond the consensus account.
strongest_objection: John 10:9 strongly supports Jesus as the saving door, while Genesis 28:17, Exodus 12:7, and Deuteronomy 6:9 support heavenly-gate and marked-post motifs. However, none of the printed excerpts identifies heaven's gates with constellations or says that the New Moon passes through them; Revelation 21 instead describes gates of the New Jerusalem. Thus the book's most distinctive extension lacks direct support from the cited texts alone.
